title: Find Champion II
statement:
A tournament has `n` teams labelled `0` to `n - 1`, and each team is a node of a directed graph. Every entry `edges[i] = [u, v]` is an edge from `u` to `v`, which says team `u` is stronger than team `v`.

A team is a champion when no other team is stronger than it. If exactly one team is a champion, return its label; if two or more teams qualify, return `-1`.

The graph has no directed cycle (it is a DAG): strength never contradicts itself, and if `a` is stronger than `b` and `b` is stronger than `c`, then `a` is stronger than `c`.
constraints: The graph has no directed cycle
notes:
## Intuition

A team is beaten by someone exactly when some edge points into it: any longer chain of "stronger than" still has to end with an edge arriving at that team. So the champions are precisely the teams with **in-degree 0**. Because the graph has no cycle, at least one such team always exists. If there is exactly one, it is the answer; if there are several, nobody is the unique champion.

A brute force could compute the full "stronger than" relation (transitive closure) and check each team, but counting incoming edges answers the same question in linear time.

## Approach

1. Make an array `indegree` of `n` zeros.
2. For each edge, add one to `indegree` of its `weaker` end (the second team).
3. Scan teams in order with `champion = -1` as "none found yet".
4. When a `team` has in-degree 0: if a champion was already found, two teams are unbeaten, so return `-1`; otherwise record `team` as `champion`.
5. Return `champion`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 3`, `edges = [[0, 1], [1, 2]]`. The edges raise `indegree` to `[0, 1, 1]`. Team 0 has in-degree 0, so `champion = 0`. Teams 1 and 2 each have an incoming edge and are skipped. The scan ends with a single unbeaten team, and the answer is `0`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m): one pass over the edges and one over the teams.
- Space: O(n) for the in-degree counts.

## Pitfalls

- Count the **second** element of each edge; the first team is the stronger one and is not beaten by this edge.
- Teams that appear in no edge at all still count: with `n = 2` and no edges both are unbeaten, so the answer is `-1`.
- Do not stop at the first in-degree-0 team; you must confirm that it is the only one.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `indegree` | for each team, how many edges point into it |
| `weaker` | the team an edge points to |
| `champion` | the unbeaten team found so far, or `-1` |
| `team` | the team being checked |

narration.2: Prepare one counter per team for the edges that point into it.
narration.3: Walk over the edges, keeping only the weaker team of each.
narration.4: That team has someone stronger than it, so raise its in-degree.
narration.6: No unbeaten team has been found yet.
narration.7: Check the teams one by one.
narration.8: No edge points into this team, so nobody is stronger: it is a champion candidate.
narration.9: A different unbeaten team was already found...
narration.10: ...so the champion is not unique: return -1.
narration.12: Remember this team as the only unbeaten one so far.
narration.15: Exactly one team had in-degree 0; return it.
